content: Fluid restriction is frequently recommended as part of the management strategy for preterm infants diagnosed with early or established bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD). The objective of this review was to evaluate whether implementing fluid restriction as a therapeutic intervention improves clinical outcomes in this population. To address this question, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Neonatal standard search strategy. Databases searched included the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE via PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL, covering studies published up to February 16, 2016. Additional sources, such as clinical trial registries, conference proceedings, and reference lists of relevant articles, were also reviewed to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized trials. The inclusion criteria for this review were prospective randomized clinical trials that compared two distinct fluid administration volumes in preterm infants with either early or established BPD. Data collection and analysis followed the standard Cochrane Neonatal methodology. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The primary outcome of interest was mortality or the need for supplemental oxygen at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age. Secondary outcomes included the duration of supplemental oxygen therapy, the proportion of infants discharged on oxygen, the duration of assisted ventilation, the length of hospital stay, weight gain, feeding tolerance, the incidence of apnea, necrotizing enterocolitis, renal dysfunction or nephrocalcinosis, lung mechanics, and the use of diuretic therapy. Only one trial met the inclusion criteria. This study involved 60 preterm infants who were 28 days old and required ongoing oxygen therapy. Participants were randomized to receive either 180 mL/kg/day of standard formula or 145 mL/kg/day of concentrated formula. However, this single study did not report data on the primary outcome of mortality or oxygen requirement at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age. Furthermore, no significant effects of fluid restriction were observed on any of the secondary outcomes assessed. The quality of evidence provided by this study was rated as low. In conclusion, there is no evidence to support the use of fluid restriction as a therapeutic intervention for preterm infants with early or established BPD.
